implementation_notes: The language absorbed both halves of the pattern: the fan-out is an array of promises and the aggregator is a combinator - allSettled for the honest wait-for-all gather (one status per recipient), any for the first successful answer, race for the first settled one, all for all-or-nothing. The deadline is AbortSignal.timeout(ms) threaded into the requests; it cannot be cancelled early, so sub-budgets or caller-driven aborts need AbortController plus setTimeout, or AbortSignal.any to combine signals. No combinator cancels the remaining work, so the loser set must be aborted explicitly with the same signal.
pitfalls: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection while the other requests keep running unobserved: use allSettled for a gather, and abort the rest yourself when all-or-nothing is intended.
Promise.any ignores rejections and short-circuits on the first fulfilment but does not cancel the losing operations; it rejects with AggregateError only when every recipient failed.
AbortSignal.timeout keeps its timer (and any listeners) alive until it fires and cannot be cancelled, so requests that finish early leave a pending timer behind.

variants.name: Hand-written counter accumulator over callback APIs
variants.idiom_name: completion counter + results array + setTimeout deadline, merge exactly once
variants.implementation_notes: Before promises existed, the aggregator was hand-written: a counter of outstanding replies, a results array indexed by recipient, and one deadline timer that flushes whatever has arrived; the merge callback runs exactly once, whichever of the two conditions fires first ('all replied' or 'budget expired'). The shape still matters when wrapping callback-style APIs, node-style emitters or legacy engines, and its correctness is entirely about that once-guard and about rejecting when nothing arrived. Promise.allSettled is the modern replacement for the same logic.
pitfalls: Without the once-guard, the deadline timer and the last callback both fire and the merge runs twice (or the timer keeps the process alive).
Per-recipient errors swallowed by the accumulator hide total failure: a gather in which every recipient failed must not merge an empty answer as if it were valid.
The counter must be decremented on every completion path, including thrown callbacks, or the gather never reaches 'all replied' and only the timer can finish it.
